title: Journal about the specific symbols from your dream
summary: Write about the images that stood out and what they might represent in your life right now.
steps: Choose one to three symbols from your dream, starting with the one that carried the most feeling.
For each, write how it looked, what it did and what you did with it in the dream.
Name the feeling around it in a word or two: calm, uneasy, tender, curious.
Ask where that same feeling appears in your life at the moment, and write whatever comes.
Close by noting one thing you understand a little better than before.
why: The Dream Code holds that meaning lives in the feeling around a symbol rather than in a fixed dictionary, so your own words are the best guide. Research on expressive writing (Pennebaker, 1997) suggests that putting experiences into words can help people make sense of them.

title: Create a visual representation of your dream scene
summary: Draw, paint or collage the scene, focusing on the emotions you felt and how the setting reflected them.
steps: Pick the scene that stayed with you most.
Gather whatever is at hand: pencils, colours, cut-out pictures or a drawing app.
Before you start, recall the feeling of the scene and choose colours and textures that match it.
Sketch the setting first, then add the figures and objects; skill does not matter.
Look at the finished image and write one sentence about something you notice now that you missed before.
why: Giving a dream a visible shape lets you see it from the outside, and the colours you choose often show the feeling more clearly than words can.

title: Practice dream re-entry
summary: Before sleep, picture yourself back in the dream with more awareness and a gentle sense of choice.
steps: Lie down comfortably and take a few slow breaths.
Recall the dream from the beginning, scene by scene, as vividly as you can.
Pause at the moment you most want to revisit and notice the details: light, sounds, textures, your feelings.
Imagine yourself there again, aware that it is a dream, and choose one small thing to explore or do differently.
Let the image fade as you drift toward sleep, and keep your journal close in case the dream returns.
why: Returning to a dream image with calm attention can deepen recall and, for some people, invite the dream to continue. If the dream was frightening, choose a calming practice instead, or rewrite its ending during the day.

title: Free association on one image
summary: Take a single image from the dream and follow wherever your thoughts lead, without judging them.
steps: Choose one small but vivid detail from the dream.
Write it at the top of a page and set a timer for five minutes.
Write every word, memory or idea it brings up, even if it seems silly or unrelated.
When the time is up, read the list and circle anything that surprises you or carries feeling.
Ask whether any circled item connects with something from the last few days.
why: Free association is the method Freud set out in The Interpretation of Dreams (1900): your own associations, not a list of symbols, lead to what an image may stand for.

title: Look for yesterday in your dream
summary: Find the fragments of the last day or two that your dream borrowed and reshaped.
steps: List the people, places, objects and conversations in the dream.
Next to each, note anything similar you saw, heard, read or thought about in the past two days.
Mark the ones that connect, and notice what the dream changed: size, setting, mood.
Ask what that change might say about how you feel about the recent event.
why: Freud called these borrowed fragments the day residue (1900), and research on the continuity hypothesis finds that dreams often reflect recent waking concerns (Domhoff, 2003).

title: Dialogue with a dream figure
summary: In a calm moment of the day, imagine a conversation with a figure from your dream.
steps: Sit somewhere quiet and recall the figure: how it looked, moved and spoke.
Write a question to it, such as: Who are you? What did you come to show me?
Write the first answer that comes, in the figure's voice, without editing.
Continue for a few exchanges, keeping your own voice kind and curious.
If the dialogue becomes distressing, stop, breathe slowly, and come back to it another day or not at all.
End by thanking the figure and noting one thing you learned.
why: Jung described a waking dialogue with inner images, which he called active imagination, in his essay The Transcendent Function (written in 1916). It is offered here gently, as a reflective exercise.

title: Amplify one dream image
summary: Explore how one striking image appears in myths, stories, art and your own culture.
steps: Pick the image that felt larger than life or strangely important.
Write what you already know about it from stories, films, songs, religion or folklore.
Look it up in a reliable book on myth or symbolism and note two or three parallels that resonate with you.
Return to the dream and ask which of these echoes fits the feeling you had.
Set aside any parallel that does not feel right; your experience is the guide.
why: Amplification is the method Jung used to widen an image with parallels from myth and culture rather than reduce it to one fixed meaning; Man and His Symbols (Jung, 1964) is an accessible introduction to his approach.

title: Meet your shadow gently
summary: Notice a dream figure you disliked or feared, and ask what quality in it might also live in you.
steps: Choose a figure in the dream who annoyed, frightened or repelled you.
Write three words that describe it, such as pushy, careless or loud.
For each word, ask honestly whether you sometimes show a little of this, or work hard never to.
Look for the hidden gift: pushy may also mean able to ask for what you need.
Write one way that quality could serve you in a healthy, measured form.
why: In Jung's psychology the shadow holds qualities we do not recognise as our own, and dreams often show them as other people (Jung, 1964). Meeting them with curiosity rather than judgement is part of what he called individuation.

title: Ask what the dream balances
summary: Consider whether the dream shows something your everyday attitude leaves out.
steps: Describe the mood of your recent days in one sentence: rushed, controlled, cautious, cheerful.
Describe the mood of the dream in one sentence.
Compare the two: is the dream the opposite, an exaggeration or a missing piece?
Write one small step that would bring a little of the dream's quality into your day.
why: Jung saw many dreams as compensatory: they bring forward what the conscious attitude neglects, offering a kind of balance (Jung, 1964).

title: Count your dream's characters and feelings
summary: Try a simple version of the Hall and Van de Castle method: list who was there, what happened and how it felt.
steps: List every character: people you know, family, strangers, animals and imaginary creatures.
Mark each interaction as friendly, aggressive or neutral, and note who started it.
Write down every emotion felt in the dream and who felt it.
Note the setting: indoors or outdoors, familiar, strange or a mix.
Keep the list with your dream; after several dreams, compare the lists and look for patterns.
why: Hall and Van de Castle (1966) developed a system for counting dream content; across many dreams, such counts often reflect a person's main relationships and concerns (Domhoff, 2003).

title: Track a recurring symbol over a week
summary: Follow one symbol through your dreams and days for a week, noting how its feeling changes.
steps: Choose a symbol that has appeared more than once in your dreams or feels important.
Each morning, note whether it appeared, in what form and with what feeling.
Each evening, note any moment when the symbol or its feeling came up during the day.
At the end of the week, read your notes and look at how the symbol's feeling has shifted.
Add what you learn to your personal symbol vocabulary in the journal.
why: The Dream Code suggests keeping a personal symbol inventory, because the way a symbol changes over time can show how you are changing. Each symbol page in DREAM CODE shows your own history with it.

title: Keep a log of a returning dream
summary: Record each return of a recurring dream and note what changes, however small.
steps: Give the recurring dream a name so you can refer to it easily.
Each time it returns, note the date, what stayed the same and what was different.
Note what was happening in your life in the days before.
Look across the entries for shifts in your role, the ending or the feeling.
If the dream is distressing and keeps returning for weeks, consider talking with a doctor or therapist.
why: Recurring dreams often accompany concerns that are still unresolved, and small changes from one return to the next can show that something is moving.

title: Rewrite the ending while awake
summary: Change a distressing dream's ending into one you can live with, then rehearse the new version in your imagination.
steps: At a calm moment of the day, not just before sleep, write a short version of the dream.
Change the ending, or any part, in whatever way feels better to you: safer, kinder, stranger or funnier.
Write the new version in the present tense, with details of what you see and feel.
Spend a few minutes each day imagining the new version.
If you wake from the old dream, ground yourself and recall the new ending.
If nightmares are frequent or disturb your sleep for weeks, a doctor or therapist trained in this approach can guide it.
why: This is inspired by imagery rehearsal, an approach studied for chronic nightmares (Krakow and Zadra, 2006). Here it is a gentle self-reflection exercise; a professional can guide the full method when nightmares are frequent.

title: Try reality checks for lucid dreaming
summary: Build a habit of asking during the day whether you are dreaming, so the question may come up in a dream.
steps: Several times a day, pause and ask yourself sincerely: am I dreaming?
Test it: read a line of text, look away and read it again, or look closely at your hands; in dreams these often change.
Take a moment to scan your surroundings for anything odd.
Link the check to cues from your own dreams, such as a recurring place or situation.
Note any lucid moments in your journal.
why: Reality testing is a long-standing lucid dreaming technique, usually most helpful alongside other methods such as MILD (Aspy and colleagues, 2017).

title: Try the MILD technique for lucid dreaming
summary: Use intention and memory as you fall back asleep to recognise your next dream as a dream.
steps: When you wake naturally from a dream, recall it in as much detail as you can.
As you settle back to sleep, repeat a phrase such as: next time I am dreaming, I will remember that I am dreaming.
Picture yourself back in the dream you just had, this time noticing a sign that it is a dream and becoming aware.
Hold the intention and the image until you fall asleep.
Record any results in your journal the next morning.
why: Mnemonic Induction of Lucid Dreams (MILD) was described by Stephen LaBerge (1980) and is among the better studied ways of encouraging lucid dreams (Stumbrys and colleagues, 2012).

title: Keep a bedside dream journal
summary: Keep a notebook by your bed and write before you do anything else on waking.
steps: Put a notebook and pen, or your phone with DREAM CODE open, within reach of your bed.
Before sleep, tell yourself that you would like to remember your dreams.
On waking, stay still for a moment with your eyes closed and let the dream come back.
Write anything you recall, even a single image or feeling, before checking messages.
Later in the day, add details and complete the entry in your journal.
why: Dreams fade quickly after waking, so writing them down at once keeps details that would otherwise be lost.

title: Record a voice memo on waking
summary: Speak your dream aloud the moment you wake, before the details fade.
steps: Keep your phone within reach, with voice input or a recorder ready.
On waking, before getting up, describe the dream aloud in the present tense.
Say the feeling first, then the images, people and places.
Later, transcribe or summarise it in your DREAM CODE journal.
why: Speaking is often quicker than writing in the first drowsy minutes, and starting with the feeling follows the book's emotion-first approach.

title: Incubate a dream before sleep
summary: Hold a question or concern in mind as you fall asleep, inviting a dream about it.
steps: Choose a question that matters to you and write it in one sentence.
Before bed, read it and spend a few minutes picturing the issue as an image.
As you fall asleep, hold the question or image gently in mind.
On waking, record whatever you dreamed, even if it seems unrelated.
Look for ways the dream might speak to your question, including through its feeling.
why: In a well-known study by Deirdre Barrett (1993), students who focused on a problem at bedtime often dreamed about it, and some found that their dreams offered useful solutions.

title: Catch the edge-of-sleep images
summary: Notice and jot down the images that appear as you drift off or come awake.
steps: Lie down for a rest with a notebook nearby, relaxed but not forcing sleep.
As you begin to drift, let images, sounds and phrases come without holding on to them.
When you surface, jot down what you saw or heard in a few words.
Later, look at the notes with curiosity; these fleeting images can be playful and creative.
If edge-of-sleep experiences frighten you, or come with being unable to move, mention them to a doctor.
why: The border between waking and sleep is rich in imagery; Lacaux and colleagues (2021) found that people who spent a short time in this earliest stage of sleep were more likely to discover a hidden rule in a puzzle afterwards.

title: Give your dream a title
summary: Sum up the dream in a few words, as if naming a film or a story.
steps: Read your dream through once more.
Write three possible titles, each no longer than six words.
Pick the one that best captures the feeling, not just the plot.
Ask what the title might also say about your life right now.
why: A title condenses a dream to its emotional core and makes it easier to spot patterns when you look back through your journal.

title: Body scan and slow breathing after a distressing dream
summary: Settle your body after a difficult dream with slow breathing and a gentle body scan.
steps: Sit or lie comfortably, with a light on if that helps you feel safe.
Breathe in slowly through your nose for a count of four and out for a count of six; repeat for a few minutes.
Bring your attention to your feet, then slowly up through your legs, belly, chest, shoulders, arms, neck and face.
Where you notice tension, breathe into it and let it soften as you breathe out.
Remind yourself where you are and that the dream is over.
If distressing dreams keep returning, consider talking with a doctor or therapist.
why: Slow breathing has been linked with feeling calmer and more relaxed (Zaccaro and colleagues, 2018), and the body scan is a core practice in mindfulness programmes (Kabat-Zinn, 1990).

title: Ground yourself with the five senses
summary: Come back to the present after an unsettling dream by noticing what you can see, feel, hear, smell and taste.
steps: Name five things you can see around you.
Name four things you can feel, such as the sheet, your feet on the floor or the air on your skin.
Name three things you can hear.
Name two things you can smell and one thing you can taste, or take a sip of water.
Finish with a slow breath and tell yourself where you are and what day it is.
why: Turning attention to the senses is a widely used way to steady yourself in the present moment after a frightening experience.

title: A small action to honour your dream
summary: Choose one small, safe and kind action in waking life that answers something your dream seemed to ask for.
steps: Ask what the dream seemed to want: rest, contact, play, creativity, care, a visit to a place.
Choose one small, concrete action that answers it, such as cooking a dish, calling someone, planting a seed or taking a walk.
Check that it is safe, affordable and kind to you and to others.
Do it within the next few days, with the dream in mind.
Afterwards, write a line about how it felt, and notice whether the dream returns or changes.
why: This is inspired by published accounts of Haudenosaunee dream teachings (Wallace, 1958), which describe honouring a dream through action in waking life. It is offered with respect, as a personal reflection, not a ceremony.

title: Tell the dream to someone you trust
summary: Share the dream aloud with a trusted person and listen to what they notice.
steps: Choose someone who listens well and will not judge or rush to explain.
Tell the dream in the present tense, including how it felt.
Ask what they noticed, what stood out and what they wonder about.
Listen without arguing; keep what resonates and let the rest go.
Afterwards, note anything you saw differently by hearing it aloud.
why: Many dream traditions value telling a dream to others. Published accounts of Haudenosaunee dream teachings describe others helping to discern what a dream wants (Wallace, 1958), and Montague Ullman developed a group approach to appreciating dreams (Ullman, 1996).

title: Write a letter to someone who has died
summary: After a dream of someone you have lost, write to them about the dream and what you would like to say.
steps: Find a quiet time and place where you can feel whatever comes.
Begin by telling them about the dream: where you were, what they did, how it felt.
Write what you miss, what you are grateful for, or what was left unsaid.
If it feels right, write a short reply in the voice you imagine they would use.
Keep the letter, read it aloud, or put it somewhere meaningful.
Be gentle with yourself afterwards; if grief feels too heavy to carry alone, reach out to someone you trust or a grief counsellor.
why: Many bereaved people keep an inner bond with those they have lost, which researchers call continuing bonds (Klass, Silverman and Nickman, 1996). Writing can give that bond a voice.

title: Savour a joyful dream with gratitude
summary: Relive the good feeling of the dream and note what it reminded you to appreciate.
steps: Close your eyes and recall the happiest moment of the dream in detail.
Notice where you feel the joy in your body and let it stay for a few breaths.
Write three things the dream reminded you to appreciate.
Choose one way to bring a little of that feeling into today.
why: Noticing and writing down what we are grateful for has been linked with greater well-being (Emmons and McCullough, 2003).

title: Sketch the map of your dream
summary: Draw the dream's places as a simple map and trace your path through them.
steps: List every place in the dream, even the ones you only passed through.
Draw them as simple shapes on a page, arranged as they felt in the dream.
Trace your route with arrows and mark where the feeling changed.
Add the people and objects you met in each place.
Look at the map: where did you want to stay, and where did you want to leave?
why: Seeing the dream's geography at a glance can reveal its structure, and some dreamers find that recurring places link up across dreams into one inner landscape.

title: Write a story or poem from your dream
summary: Use the dream as raw material for a short piece of creative writing.
steps: Choose the scene or image with the most energy.
Write freely for ten minutes, letting the story go wherever it wants, beyond what you dreamed.
Try a different point of view: a dream figure, an object or the place itself.
Shape what you wrote into a short story, poem or letter.
Notice what the writing adds to your understanding of the dream.
why: Writing creatively from a dream lets you explore it without having to explain it, and often brings out feelings that analysis misses.

title: Sleep routine basics
summary: Support restful sleep and clearer dream recall with a steady, calming evening routine.
steps: Go to bed and get up at roughly the same times each day.
Give yourself a quiet wind-down before bed, with dim lights and less screen time.
Keep your bedroom cool, dark and comfortable.
Notice how caffeine, alcohol and late heavy meals affect your sleep and your dreams.
If you have ongoing trouble sleeping, frequent nightmares or strong daytime sleepiness, talk to a doctor.
why: Regular, calm sleep habits support restful sleep for many people. This is general wellness information, not medical advice.

title: Name the feeling first
summary: Start with the emotion of the dream, then see how the images formed around it.
steps: Before thinking about any symbol, write one word for the main feeling of the dream.
Add any other feelings and the point in the dream where each one arrived.
List the images that sat closest to each feeling.
Ask where you have felt the same emotion in waking life recently.
why: The Dream Code holds that emotion comes first and the image forms around it, so naming the feeling is often the quickest way into a dream's meaning.

title: Name what is following you
summary: For dreams of being chased or hurried, explore what in waking life feels as if it is catching up with you.
steps: Describe the pursuer or the pressure in a few words, including how close it felt.
Write what you were running toward or away from in the dream.
List anything in waking life you have been putting off, avoiding or racing to keep up with.
Choose one small, manageable step toward the item that feels most pressing.
Only if it feels comfortable, imagine turning to face the pursuer from a safe distance and asking what it wants; write the answer.
why: Pursuit is one of the four emotional patterns described in The Dream Code. One modern proposal, threat simulation theory, suggests that chase dreams may rehearse responses to danger (Revonsuo, 2000).

title: Carry the feeling of lift into your day
summary: For dreams of flying, climbing or rising, recall the feeling of lift and bring it into waking life.
steps: Recall the moment of rising: what lifted you, how high you went, what you saw.
Name the feeling: freedom, mastery, relief, perhaps a touch of dizziness.
Ask where in waking life you are rising, or would like to.
Choose a small physical cue, such as a deep breath and a taller posture, to recall the feeling during the day.
why: Ascent is one of the four emotional patterns described in The Dream Code, which holds that the rising feeling matters more than the image that carries it.

title: Find your footing
summary: For dreams of falling or sinking, explore where waking life feels unsteady and what supports you.
steps: Describe the fall or descent: how it began, how fast it was, how it ended.
Name where in waking life you feel unsupported, uncertain or let down at the moment.
List the people, habits and places that steady you.
Choose one support to lean on this week, and note how it feels.
Notice, too, whether the descent felt like going deeper into something worth exploring.
why: Descent is one of the four emotional patterns described in The Dream Code. Falling is among the dream themes people report most often (Nielsen and colleagues, 2003).

title: Explore the new room
summary: For dreams of discovering new rooms or widening spaces, explore what new possibility the space could stand for.
steps: Describe the new space: how you found it, its size, its light and what it held.
Name the feeling of discovering it: wonder, excitement, unease, relief.
Ask what part of your life has recently gained room: a skill, a relationship, an interest.
Write one way you could step a little further into that new space this week.
why: Expansion is one of the four emotional patterns described in The Dream Code; finding unknown rooms in a familiar house is a dream many people recognise.

title: Notice where the dream lives in your body
summary: Explore what your body did and felt in the dream, and what it feels now.
steps: Recall what your body was doing in the dream: running, floating, frozen, held, warm or cold.
Sit quietly and notice whether any trace of that feeling is present now, and where.
Rest a hand there and breathe slowly for a minute.
Ask what this part of you might need today: rest, movement, warmth or a stretch.
Write a line about what you noticed.
why: Dreams are felt as well as seen. Published accounts of Haudenosaunee dream teachings describe the body taking part in dreams (Wallace, 1958), and the book's emotion-first view begins with how a dream felt.

title: Reflect on closeness and boundaries
summary: After an intimate dream, explore privately what it says about connection, desire and comfort.
steps: Write privately; this reflection is for you alone.
Note the feeling the dream left: warmth, longing, surprise or discomfort.
Ask what quality the other person stood for, such as confidence, tenderness or freedom, rather than who they were.
Consider what the dream suggests about the closeness you want, or the boundaries that matter to you.
Remember that intimate dreams are common and are not instructions; they often speak about connection in symbolic ways.
why: Reading a dream figure for the qualities it represents, rather than taking the scene literally, is a long-standing approach in dream work and keeps the focus on what you need.

title: Note it, date it, revisit it
summary: For dreams that feel like glimpses of the future, record them carefully and look back later with an open mind.
steps: Write the dream down as soon as you can, with the date and every detail you remember.
Note why it felt different from ordinary dreams: vividness, certainty, a particular feeling.
Write what you were worried about or hoping for in waking life at the time.
Set a reminder to reread it in a month, and note what you think then.
Avoid making important decisions on the strength of the dream alone.
why: Many people report dreams that seem to anticipate events. Writing them down at once keeps an accurate record, since memories of dreams can shift over time.

title: Carry a comforting image through the day
summary: Bring a soothing image from your dream into a calm moment, as a source of steadiness.
steps: Choose the image from your dream that felt most comforting or healing.
Sit quietly and picture it in detail, with its colours, sounds and warmth.
Notice how your breathing and body respond.
Give the image a word or phrase you can recall later.
Return to it for a few breaths in a stressful moment.
why: Holding a calming image in mind is a familiar way to relax, and an image your own dream gave you can feel especially personal.
